page.desc: Jackery's current power stations compared by today's US store price, cost per watt-hour, weight and the output named reviewers measured, with the right pick for each need.
page.answer: Short answer. Which Jackery power station should I buy? For most homes, the Explorer 2000 v2: $999 for 2,042 Wh is $0.49 per Wh, tied for the lowest in Jackery's store today, and GearLab measured 1,710 Wh out. Buy the Explorer 5000 Plus only for 240 V circuits from one box.

page.after:
What the differences mean

Dealectric does not test units. Every measured figure on this page comes from the named reviewer. Prices are from Jackery's US store, read 2026-11-15.

  • Explorer 2000 v2: $999 ÷ 2,042 Wh = $0.49 per rated Wh. On OutdoorGearLab's measured 1,710 Wh it is $999 ÷ 1,710 = $0.58 per delivered Wh. Weight: 2,042 Wh ÷ 39.5 lb = 51.7 Wh/lb.
  • Explorer 1500 Ultra against it: $1,079 − $999 = $80 more for 2,042 − 1,536 = 506 Wh less, and only 39.5 − 38.6 = 0.9 lb lighter. $1,079 ÷ 1,536 = $0.70 per Wh. 1,536 ÷ 38.6 = 39.8 Wh/lb (weight from Newsshooter).
  • HomePower 1000 Plus v2 vs HomePower 1000 v2: $669 ÷ 1,024 = $0.65 vs $549 ÷ 1,024 = $0.54 per Wh. The Plus costs $669 − $549 = $120 more for 1,800 − 1,500 = 300 W more output and the option of up to five 2 kWh packs. Gizmodo's 14% idle loss works out to 0.14 × 1,024 = 143 Wh a day.
  • HomePower 3600 Plus: $1,899 ÷ 3,584 = $0.53 per Wh. 3,584 ÷ 77 = 46.5 Wh/lb. The Solar Lab's 34 W idle × 24 h = 816 Wh a day with the inverter left on.
  • Explorer 5000 Plus: 5,040 Wh ÷ 134.5 lb (61 kg) = 37.5 Wh/lb. HOBOTECH's 85 W idle × 24 h = 2,040 Wh, which is 2,040 ÷ 4,450 = 46% of the energy HOBOTECH measured from a full battery. The Solar Lab measured a lower 58 W.
  • Explorer 1000 v2: 910 ÷ 1,070 = 85% of rated reached the outlets in GearLab's test. 1,070 ÷ 24.4 = 43.9 Wh/lb. Amazon's listing title gives 1,024 Wh, while Notebookcheck and GearLab give 1,070 Wh.

Four more current models had no measured figure from a named reviewer that we could read, so they appear here instead of in the table: the Explorer 1500 v2 ($849 ÷ 1,536 = $0.55 per Wh; 1,536 ÷ 31.97 lb = 48.0 Wh/lb), the Explorer 1000 Plus ($619 ÷ 1,264 = $0.49 per Wh), the Explorer 300D ($209 ÷ 288 = $0.73 per Wh; 288 ÷ 5.5 lb = 52.4 Wh/lb) and the Explorer 300 ($289 ÷ 292 = $0.99 per Wh).

Why cost per Wh and Wh per pound decide it

The capacity on the label is the battery's rating. Not all of it reaches your appliance. OutdoorGearLab got 84% of rated out of the 2000 v2 and 85% out of the 1000 v2, and HOBOTECH got 88% out of the 5000 Plus. Dividing the store price by rated Wh shows what each unit charges you for stored energy. Dividing Wh by weight shows how much you carry for that energy. On both counts the Explorer 2000 v2 comes out ahead of every 1.5 kWh-plus Jackery in the table. The 1500 Ultra charges a premium for weatherproofing, not for energy. The 5000 Plus has the lowest Wh per pound in the table, because you are paying for its 240 V inverter and 4,000 W solar input.

Switchover time matters if you plan to use the station as a UPS for a PC. An ATX 3.1 power supply only has to ride through 12 ms of lost AC at full load (Seasonic). Jackery rates both HomePower 1000 models at under 10 ms, which is inside that window. The Explorer 1000 v2 (20 ms, Notebookcheck) and the Explorer 2000 v2 (under 20 ms, Jackery) are not. For a fridge or lights, the gap makes no difference.

Idle draw matters in a long outage with small loads. With the inverter on, the 5000 Plus burns 58–85 W doing nothing, and The Solar Lab could not reliably start an air conditioner with a 10,000 W start-up surge. For a CPAP, router and fridge over several days, another brand wins: Andrew Riha for pv magazine measured about 10 W idle on the Anker SOLIX S5000 (pv magazine) {buy:anker-solix-s5000}.

Not recommended

Explorer 1000 Plus, if you're buying it to expand later. It ties the 2000 v2 at $0.49 per Wh, but Jackery's own product page says the Battery Pack 1000 Plus has been discontinued. That leaves its expand-to-5 kWh claim with no pack to buy, and it is rated for 4,000 cycles, against 6,000 on the HomePower v2 models.
